title: MFA bypass CONFIRMED at runtime on the OAuth authorize endpoint — and a SECOND bug is the only thing currently stopping it. Fixing that second bug arms the first.
bluf: The agent proved it with a control, on a throwaway account it created, with MFA enabled on that account alone. Same account, same password: POST /api/auth/login returns 403 MFA_REQUIRED and zero tokens. POST /api/oauth/authorize returns 302 with a valid authorization code. MFA, lockout and account status are all bypassed at the authorize step, and the stored code carries no PKCE gate either. That is KS-781, and it is now confirmed at runtime rather than inferred from a code read. THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST IS WHAT IT FOUND NEXT. The leaked code does not currently become a token - exchanging it returns 400 User not found. The agent predicted a clean token pair, was wrong, and chased the 400 instead of reporting the bypass and moving on. The cause is a separate bug, filed KS-790: the token leg calls a post-auth RLS-scoped lookup inside a pre-auth flow, so it fails for EVERY authorization_code grant. So a broken OAuth grant is the only thing standing between the bypass and a working token. FIXING KS-790 IN ISOLATION RE-OPENS THE BYPASS END TO END. A working token exchange with no MFA check on authorize is strictly worse than a broken one. The agent has said so on both tickets and marked KS-790 blocked-behind KS-781, but that is a comment on a board, and anyone triaging KS-790 as a routine broken-OAuth bug could fix it without reading it.

title: The scopes report is in: it reads message bodies, and 3 of 7 permissions are write/send. Grant, or not?
bluf: Prior-rulings check: you ruled attio-entra-consent-m365 => scopes-first at 07:07. This is that report coming back, and it is the decision you deferred. Full document: 5_Project_History/2026-09-07_attio-m365-scopes-report.md. THE ANSWER TO WHAT YOU ASKED: yes, something reads message BODIES - Mail.Read and Mail.ReadWrite cover the full message including attachments, and Attio stores bodies rather than headers alone. AND IT IS NOT READ-ONLY: three of the seven are write or send - Mail.ReadWrite modifies mailbox items, and Mail.Send plus SMTP.Send send mail AS the connected user, recipients seeing it from them. A reasonable person reading "email and calendar sync" would not expect send-as. Plus offline_access, which turns a session into standing access: Attio holds a refresh token and keeps working with nobody watching until someone revokes it. THE REASSURING HALF, with its limit: the permissions look DELEGATED not application-level, on three independent indications - so a mailbox reaches Attio only when its owner connects it, and admin consent removes the "needs admin approval" prompt rather than handing over every mailbox in Datasec. BUT the agent named the gap rather than smoothing it: Microsoft grants what is REGISTERED ON THE APP, not only what is in the URL, so if Attio also declares application-level permissions the same consent grants those too and this report would not know. THE TEN-SECOND CHECK THAT BEATS THE WHOLE REPORT: the consent screen itself is the authority. It labels application-level permissions distinctly - "without a signed-in user" or "Read mail in all mailboxes". If any line says ALL MAILBOXES, the delegated reading is wrong and you stop. Also unmeasured and worth knowing: Attios data retention after a mailbox is disconnected is undocumented in what was read - whether stored bodies are deleted. The agent says that is the one it would most want answered before consenting, and it belongs in the security pack you already ruled to send.

title: Round 3 did NOT close the SEC-01 Blocker — the builder and the gate proved it independently, and the round also opened a new Major. Your bent cap is spent and the next move is a design call, not another narrow fix.
bluf:
**OVERRIDE:** Kam ruled `round3` at 18:58 on the stated premise that it would close the Blocker. **This card is that round's RESULT, not a re-raise of it.**

**ROUND 3 IS A NO GO.** Two independent instruments reached it, and they agree.

**FOUND.** The fix rests on `firstRunComplete` being written only beside `authEnforced`. It is also written by the FRONTEND wizard at three sites that have nothing to do with authentication — when the Log Analytics connection test succeeds, when data validation passes, and when the admin ticks 'don't show this guide again'. The wizard's own tab order puts Log Analytics Access BEFORE User Access, so **the bricking path is the intended journey, not an edge case.** Ticking the checkbox alone is sufficient. Any restart in that gap — scale-to-zero, a revision recycle, an image update, going home for the night — and every route 503s, `/first-run-setup` redirects to `/login`, and `POST /api/auth/enforce`, the one route that could write the missing key, is itself refused. Only exit is hand-editing settings.json on the customer's volume.

**AND ROUND 3 OPENED SOMETHING NEW (F-2, Major).** A deployment that HAD auth enforced, whose settings.json is emptied with the backup layer also gone, now serves **open mode across all 175 routes** where round 2 denied. That is SEC-01's own direction of failure, reintroduced by the fix for SEC-01.

**WHAT GENUINELY CLOSED, recorded as closing:** F-B / M10 is real — mutating the sole producer fails exactly cell D and restore returns 23/23, proved by contrast rather than assertion. The single-write-site premise was verified across all 678 tracked files. 2177/2177, 113 suites, 0 skips, reproduced independently.

**TESTED.** A 2x2 matrix on a real server — real `npm start`, real DATA_DIR, boot then interrupt then boot on the same directory — across both heads and both variants. The deadlock was driven with a VALID CSRF token. F-2 was measured as a before/after table on the same two heads. NOT tested: behaviour on Azure Files or Container Apps (local disk is not a network mount), and whether a real incident removes the backups while sparing the sentinel — the gate names that as F-2's weakest link itself.

**HOW.** Positive control on the instrument (`/api/health` 200 on every boot of both heads, so a 503 elsewhere is a gate decision and not a dead server). Negative control that flips with the subject (`/api/__qa_impossible__` returns 404 when the gate is open, 503 when closed). Positive control on the module (the function throws 'is not a function' on the before-head, proving the before column is really before-head code). Every tamper asserted to have LANDED before its effect was read; a 403-CSRF run was discarded rather than reported. The gate found and fixed two of its own harness bugs before recording any claim, and over-read F-2 initially and narrowed it. Report and evidence: `!CODING/Testing Agent MAIN/projects/nexusai/reports/2026-09-07-rd361-round3-tier1/`

**WEDNESDAY'S READING, marked as inference and NOT measured by the gate:** rounds 2 and 3 both tried to *discriminate* 'never set up' from 'set up then lost'. The gate has now shown those two states are **byte-identical** by the time the check runs, because JsonStorage's constructor normalises a missing or corrupt settings.json to `{}` before the gate ever reads it. If that holds, **no discriminator built on settings.json content can work**, and a round 4 aimed at a better discriminator is spending your cap on something structurally unavailable. The deadlock itself looks like the more tractable target. This is Wednesday's reasoning, not a measurement — it needs a round to test it before anyone builds on it.

**Nothing is merged, nothing is deployed, nothing degrades overnight.**

title: All four measured as you asked — none reachable in our code today, and my recommendation is to BUMP rather than accept them
bluf: ACTION: tap an option below, and if you tap bump, say yes to one registry lookup so I can confirm fixed versions exist. Nobody can push to Secuura until this lands - not us, not Peter, not Stuart. WHAT YOU ASKED FOR, DELIVERED: you ruled measure-then-rule; here are all four together. GHSA-2x7j (HIGH, nodemailer) is UNREACHABLE - the quadratic blow-up needs a crafted address LIST, and every attacker-reachable path validates to a SINGLE address first (z.string().email() at auth.ts:145, isEmail() at certifications.ts:991); the one fallback that looked unguarded, notificationClient.ts:99, is guarded BY ITS CALLER, which the seat chased specifically because it looked like the hole. GHSA-wmmp and GHSA-cc9r are MOOT - the recipient allow-list they bypass, EMAIL_RECIPIENT_ALLOWLIST, is NOT configured; empty in both services, live secuura-auth reports len=0 against three known-set controls (NODE_ENV 11, DATABASE_URL 80, JWT_PUBLIC_KEY 600), so there is nothing in force to bypass. GHSA-jxfw (morgan) is THEORETICAL on three independent grounds, any one sufficient - the strongest is that Node decodes HTTP headers as latin1, so a U+2028 in a User-Agent arrives as mojibake and the vector cannot deliver the character at all. AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER SENTENCE TO YOU: I told you morgan sits in ten production services including auth, the gateway and security. DECLARED in ten, IMPORTED in three - queue, guardian and demo-service. The three I named to make it sound worst are exactly the three that never call it. That embellishment was mine, not the seat's; its number was a declaration count and it said so. THE THREE CAVEATS, CARRIED AS CAVEATS RATHER THAN SMOOTHED AWAY, and the first is the seat's own sentence and the reason for my recommendation: unreachable because of a property we happen to hold, not because the vulnerable code is absent. We SHIP all four packages. The two allow-list ones flip the moment ANY deployment sets EMAIL_RECIPIENT_ALLOWLIST - a CONFIG change, not a code change, and nobody setting it would think they were touching security. Second: this is bounded to LOCAL config; the demo VM's environment was NOT read, so if the demo has the allow-list on, those two stop being moot for it. Third: whether a single PATHOLOGICAL address could also be slow is UNMEASURED - the reported vector is closed, that residual is not. And morgan is theoretical UNDER THE SINK WE HAVE TODAY, never 'not a bug': Python's splitlines() DOES split on U+2028 (measured, 2 parts vs control 1) and JSON.stringify does NOT escape it, so the day those logs reach a Python-based processor it becomes real with no change to our code. FINALLY, THE THING I WOULD RATHER TELL YOU THAN ROUTE AROUND: your 08:12 grant STILL does not cover these. Its clause 2 tests whether a package reaches a shipped image, and all four do. What was measured is that the vulnerable PATH is not exercised - a better fact, and a DIFFERENT one. So it stays your ruling, and your clause is slightly blunter than the question turned out to be.

title: Unauthenticated cross-tenant billing read via the /originate/ nginx bypass — measured locally; demo and production UNMEASURED
bluf: MEASURED BY THE SECUURA SEAT ON THE LOCAL STACK, with controls in both directions: GET /originate/api/metering/usage returns tenant billing data with NO credential, when two client-supplied headers (x-user-role: connector, x-tenant-id) are sent. title: Your demo fix deployed, reloaded cleanly — and did NOTHING. A single-file bind mount binds the INODE. Closing it needs a container recreate, which your ruling excluded
bluf: YOUR OWN VERIFICATION CRITERION IS THE ONLY REASON WE KNOW THIS. Everything looked right: the config uploaded with a matching checksum, `nginx -t` exit 0 BEFORE the reload, `nginx -s reload` exit 0, container still `Up 2 days (healthy)`. A seat that reported on those signals would have told you the exposure was closed. HALF 1 OF YOUR PAIR FAILED: the credential-free GET returns 401 FROM ORIGINATE, not 404 — which proves the request is still being proxied there. THE EXPOSURE IS OPEN, exactly as it was this morning. HALF 2 IS GREEN so this is NOT an outage: /health, /, /verify/, /admin/ all 200; /api/documents 401 with auth working; the sibling /analytics/ route untouched. The box is fully functional and in the state it was in before anyone touched it. THE CAUSE, MEASURED TO THE INODE RATHER THAN THEORISED: a single-FILE bind mount binds the INODE, not the path. Host file sha ae4cc54c, inode 1311680, 32831 bytes; container sha 265b7a60, inode 1311687, 31596 bytes. The copy replaced the file and produced a NEW inode; the mount still resolves to the original, so nginx reloaded and faithfully re-read the OLD file. And that old inode is now UNLINKED — `find -inum 1311687` returns 0 paths, against a control where `find -inum 1311680` does return its path. SO NO HOST-SIDE WRITE CAN REACH WHAT THAT CONTAINER IS SERVING. Only recreating the container re-resolves the mount. WHOSE ERROR THIS IS, PLAINLY: the seat told Wednesday the file was bind-mounted so an rsync plus a reload would do it, Wednesday passed that to you as the cheap-and-reversible framing, and it is the basis your authorisation rested on. The file IS bind-mounted; what does not follow is that replacing it on the host reaches the container. Wednesday's provenance line at the time said it had not read the demo host and was relying on the seat — that qualification was correct and it is not a defence. The project's own documented redeploy path (`rsync` then `docker compose build && up -d`) works precisely because `up -d` recreates the container; the trap is specific to the shortcut. WHAT IS NEEDED: `docker compose up -d nginx-gateway` in /home/secuura/secuura/Dev. That is a SERVICE RESTART on the demo box, which your ruling explicitly excluded, so the seat stopped and did not do it. Seconds of gateway downtime; rollback held at /home/secuura/nginx-demo.conf.rollback-ks1041-20260910, verified byte-identical to the original. ONE THING TO KNOW BEFORE YOU CHOOSE: the seat left the HOST file as the KS-1041 version rather than restoring it, so the correct config is staged. The consequence, said out loud rather than discovered later: the NEXT `docker compose up -d` on that box, for any reason, by anyone, will apply this change without whoever runs it intending it then. It is the desired change, so it is not dangerous — but nobody should meet it as a surprise.
default_action: HOLD. The demo keeps the open route — an unauthenticated read of tenant billing data on the box prospects and the team reach — and Step 2 stays blocked behind Step 1's verification. Nothing degrades and nothing is customer-facing; production does not exist, measured. The staged host file stays staged, so the fix lands whenever that container is next recreated for any other reason.

title: The demo hole is shut from OUTSIDE and open from INSIDE — 34 containers can forge connector identity to originate and get a 200. Step 2 is bigger than the card you ruled, and it needs a fresh seat
bluf: OVERRIDE REASON, STATED AS THE MEASUREMENT. The gate will match `secuura-ks1041-fix-shape-demo-exposed` (ruled `both-sequenced` today at 10:32). That ruling stands and Step 1 is DELIVERED AND VERIFIED. This card exists because measuring Step 2's premise DISPROVED it: the card told you Step 2 would 'make the route's premise true instead of assumed', and the premise is already true at the gateway and false somewhere nobody had looked. WHAT IS MEASURED, with controls in both directions: probing from `secuura-verifier-frontend`, a container with no business reaching originate — direct to `originate:4000` with NO headers returns 401, and with a forged `x-user-role: connector` + `x-tenant-id` returns **200**. Through `api-gateway:8080` the SAME forged request returns 401. Both no-header cells are 401, so the difference is the headers and not the path; both gateway cells are 401, so the gateway's strip is doing exactly what its code says. Reachability was confirmed by probe rather than inferred: `originate:4000/health` 200, positive control `api-gateway:8080/health` 200 proving the tool works, discriminating control `zzz-no-such-service` no response proving a 200 means something. THE BOUNDARY, AS PRECISE AS THE FINDING — this is NOT externally reachable: `originate:4000` is not published to the host (control: `nginx-gateway` IS, at `0.0.0.0:6882->80/tcp`). It sits on one flat network, `dev_secuura-network`, `Internal: false`, with **34 containers**, every one of which can address it directly. So: shut from the internet, open to any peer container on the demo box. WHAT THIS BREAKS. The seat's own scope proposal, which it retracted within twenty minutes of writing it: it had said 'the header is not the vulnerability; the ungated path to it was' and told me explicitly NOT to touch `extractTenantContext`. That reasoning holds only for gateway traffic. On the direct path the same header is attacker-controlled, and `extractTenantContext` (`index.ts:230`) reads it UNCONDITIONALLY, before any auth. So the fix cannot be a per-route patch on the metering shim — the shim is one consumer of a trust that is unverified at the door. THE CORRECT SHAPE: originate establishes that a request came from the gateway before honouring ANY trust header — one early middleware. Bigger than the one-file change proposed, far smaller than the seven services that read these headers. KEPT SEPARATE, DELIBERATELY: the metering 200 is MEASURED. That the same door is open wider — including a cross-tenant read — is REASONED. Confirming it needs a valid JWT and a probe nobody has run, and the seat refused to run it without a fresh commission. NOTHING IS BUILT, no Step 2 branch exists, and the seat wrapped rather than start an auth-path change on a thin margin.
default_action: HOLD. Step 1's fix stands and the route stays shut from outside. The internal bypass remains: any of 34 containers on the demo box can read tenant billing data without a credential. Nothing customer-facing is exposed — production does not exist, measured earlier today — and nothing degrades while this waits. The cost of silence is that a hardening fix sits undone on a box the team and prospects reach.

title: Kintsugi is 322 commits behind and has never been touched since it was built — 'bring it current' is a 1.5-2h whole-estate rebuild, not a catch-up. Your call on WHEN, not whether
bluf: YOUR 13:22 RULING IS DISCHARGED IN SCOPE — this is WHEN, plus one scope question the measurement exposed. WHAT WAS MEASURED: kintsugi has not been touched since it was built (source rsynced 2026-08-19, images built that night, nothing since). 322 commits behind, 162 touching a deployable surface, 31 images invalidated because packages/shared changed, 5 migrations behind. Sizing from evidence: this box's own cold build took 1h27m, read from the images' CreatedAt. THE TRAP THAT MATTERED IS CLEAR: KS-535 is fine — kintsugi has its own wallet AND its own Blockfrost credentials, so the failure that cost 295 local and 2 demo anchors cannot bite. Box healthy, 18h up, zero unhealthy. FINDING 1 — THERE IS NO ROLLBACK, AND THAT IS WORSE THAN I FIRST WROTE. All 31 images are tagged bare "latest", there are ZERO dangling images, and no rollback script or previous-image record exists anywhere. A build overwrites the latest tag and nobody records the old IDs, so rollback today means rebuilding from old source — another ~1.5 hours. THE FIX COSTS SECONDS: re-tag all 31 as pre-DATE before building. A tag is a pointer, not a copy — zero disk, under a second — and it turns rollback from a 1.5-hour rebuild into 31 docker tag commands plus one restart, about two minutes. Corollary now in bold in the runbook: NO docker prune at any point, because the 29 GB cache is the only rollback material that exists. FINDING 2 — I AM CORRECTING MY OWN RECOMMENDATION ON THIS CARD. I told you overnight was risky because a half-rebuilt estate is worse than a stale one. The ordering the seat worked out dissolves that, because docker build is non-destructive: Phase 0 tag (seconds), Phase 1 rsync, Phase 2 BUILD ALL 31 (~1.5-2h) with NOTHING SWAPPED so a failure there costs nothing, Phase 3 migrations, Phase 4 swap one at a time with a health read. The dangerous window shrinks from ~90 minutes to about two. Overnight is now materially safer than when I argued against it. And the migration ordering is settled on a MECHANISM rather than a principle: 046 and 047 add CHECK constraints, and 047's own comment records that old code demonstrably writes outside the set (a POST to /api/oauth/apps with appType native that used to return 201) — so migrations-first would turn a silent success into a violation. Migrations-LAST is also wrong, because 044 adds five columns the new code expects. Build-first resolves both. HONEST LIMIT CARRIED: none of the five migrations ships a down-migration, so a full rollback leaves old code under the new constraints; dropping the two by name is written as an ESCALATION, not a mid-flight decision. FINDING 3 — THE SCOPE QUESTION, AND IT IS YOURS: DEMO RUNS guardian AND queue. KINTSUGI HAS NEITHER — no container and no image. Demo has them because they were started once in July under a phase2 profile and never stopped. So "bring kintsugi up to date" does not say whether it means MATCH DEVELOP or MATCH DEMO, and those differ by two services. A dev box missing two services demo runs cannot reproduce a demo problem, which is the whole point of your kintsugi-first ruling — so I recommend including them — but it widens what you authorised, so it is yours. And it makes a known trap live: compose treats those two as orphans, so --remove-orphans would delete them once kintsugi has them. ALSO DONE, no decision needed: your kintsugi-first ruling is now a comment on KS-601 rather than living only in your email; the runbook is PR #943; and the Stuart/Peter notice is drafted in TWO versions and HELD — one that raises the UAT-label question plainly, one that is deploy facts only. Nothing deployed, no migration applied, no contact with Stuart or Peter.
